vopros: What do foreign nationals need to buy a home in Los Angeles?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Yes. Foreign nationals can generally buy residential real estate in Los Angeles, including people who are not U.S. citizens or green-card holders. Immigration status and property ownership are separate issues; the bigger differences are financing, tax treatment, and documentation.

For a typical purchase, you'll need:

- Identification: Usually a valid foreign passport. Your escrow/title company and lender, if any, will have their own identity-verification requirements.
- Purchase funds: For an all-cash purchase, you'll need documented funds that can be wired into a U.S. escrow account. Banks and escrow/title companies may require documentation showing the source of the money for compliance purposes.
- Financing, if applicable: You don't necessarily need a U.S. green card to get a mortgage, but conventional U.S. financing can be difficult without U.S. income and credit history. Some lenders offer "foreign national" mortgages, typically with different underwriting and potentially larger down-payment requirements.
- Tax identification: You do not necessarily need an SSN or ITIN simply to own a house. An ITIN becomes relevant when you have a U.S. federal tax purpose, such as reporting taxable U.S. income or dealing with taxes when selling the property. The IRS specifically provides ITIN procedures for foreign owners/sellers of U.S. real estate. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/itin-guidance-for-foreign-property-buyers-sellers?utm_source=openai))
- Escrow/title: California purchases normally go through escrow, with a preliminary title report, deed, disclosures and other closing documents. ([dre.ca.gov](https://www.dre.ca.gov/Consumers/FirstHomeCalifornia.html?utm_source=openai))
- Closing funds: In addition to the purchase price/down payment, budget for title/escrow charges, inspections, lender expenses if financing, property taxes, insurance and other closing expenses.

One important point is that buying a Los Angeles home does not itself give you a U.S. visa, residency, a green card, or the right to live or work in the United States. Similarly, an ITIN is a tax number and does not confer immigration status or work authorization. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc857?utm_source=openai))

Taxes deserve particular attention for foreign buyers. If you rent the property, U.S. and California tax obligations can arise. When you eventually sell, FIRPTA can require federal withholding where the seller is a foreign person, and California has its own real-estate withholding regime. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/firpta-withholding?utm_source=openai)) This makes getting the ownership structure right before purchasing—individual name versus an LLC, corporation, trust, etc.—particularly important for foreign buyers.

If you tell me your citizenship/residence country, whether you're buying all-cash or with a mortgage, and roughly the purchase price (e.g. $1M, $3M, $10M), I can lay out exactly what you'd need and the likely tax/financing considerations for a Los Angeles purchase.
